utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, arising from the rulings recently received and from one or two other events, there are a few comparatively minor, or indeed very minor, administrative matters I'd like to raise. Looking at the number of them and realising that for one I'd like to have a draft motion available for you to consider, a motion that brings us up-to-date with witnesses, may I address you a little later this morning, at the beginning or end of one of the breaks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to deal with it now, but I think it probably better if I deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While it's in my mind, let me mention something which we've been considering; the timetable. If we finish this part earlier than we'd thought, and it appears we may, then we'd be minded to bring forward Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that confirmation of a position you had articulated earlier. My best estimate at the moment is that we probably will finish next Monday or Tuesday and I'm working on the basis, as you had indicated earlier, that the start of Croatia would be a fortnight from the end date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll have the witness, please. May we have the senior legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take at seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the interest of assisting the members of the public who may not speak Albanian, I've provided a piece of paper with the correct spelling of the witness's name. Examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Behar Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Haxhiavdija, were you born on the 24th of June, 1960, in the town of Gjakove in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you the son of Mr. Ismet Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1999, did you provide a statement to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 7th of May in the year 2001, did you provide an additional statement to a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th of January this year, 2002, in the country where you now reside, were you provided with copies of the statements that you previously made to the Office of the Prosecutor in a language that you understand in the presence of a member of the Office of the Prosecutor and a person qualified to witness your declaration?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you confirm that the copies of your statement were true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I will ask that the statements of Mr. Haxhiavdija be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. However, before numbers are assigned, I would ask Your Honours that we go into private session very briefly to discuss a matter related to a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. We're now in open session. The original version will be marked number -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 303, under seal. The redacted -- the first redacted version will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 303A, under seal, and the public redacted version will be 303B.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, Behar Haxhiavdija is a 42-year-old Kosovo Albanian Muslim man who, prior to the events of 1999, was a manager of a wine factory in the municipality of Gjakove. On the evening of 1 April 1999, Mr. Haxhiavdija, his wife, and three small children were staying at the compound of Mr. Haxhiavdija's brother-in-law, Mr. Lulezim Vejsa, which is located at 157 Milos Gilic Street. Other family members sought shelter in the same compound. There was a pool hall with a basement in this compound, and at night the women and children slept in this basement. The men kept watch and slept in the house. The men had devised a plan to escape from the compound in case Serb forces tried to break in. It was believed that while Serb forces might attack Kosovo Albanian males, they would not harm women and children. So Mr. Haxhiavdija, his brother-in-law Lulezim Vejsa, and Mr. Hani Hoxha had an escape route planned, if necessary. On the night of 1st April, there were 21 people sleeping in the basement. All were women and children with the exception of Hysen Gashi, a man who was mentally ill. Just after midnight, Mr. Haxhiavdija heard the sound of rifling action of a firearm; the distinctive metallic sound that is made when a person moves the action of the rifle to send a bullet into the chamber of a weapon. Mr. Haxhiavdija returned to the house and woke up his brother-in-law. They heard a voice say in the Serbian language, "Open the door," and then they heard a vehicle trying to push through the gate. Mr. Haxhiavdija and Lulezim Vejsa passed through their escape route and left the compound. They spent the rest of the night hiding in another home. They could hear the sound of gunfire and explosions and could see that houses were burning. In the morning of 2nd of April, Mr. Haxhiavdija returned to the Vejsa compound and found it full of burning rubble. He learned that members of the Serb police had killed his wife and three children as well as other members of his extended family who had taken shelter in the basement the night before. Later that day, Mr. Haxhiavdija joined a convoy and went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You gave two statements to different investigators, one on the 15th of April, 1999, and the second two years later on May 7th, 2001; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume -- or I'm asking you whether your first statement is more complete and closer to the truth, in view of the fact that you gave it immediately after the events that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Both are the same, in fact, with a small change, because the second statement was given after quite a long period, and it may have been that things were forgotten or just fall from my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your father give a statement to the investigators two days after your second statement, on the 9th of May, 2001, to the same investigator that you gave your statement to? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that your father gave a statement two days after your second statement, on the 9th of May, 2001, to the same investigator?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 2nd of April, 1999, around midnight?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I was in Lulezim Vejsa's house, my brother-in-law. He's my wife's brother. That's where I was at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your first statement, you claim that you were on guard, that you were watching and waiting. Who was keeping watch?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: We were almost all there. We were awake, and we were keeping watch for anything that might happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your second statement, you say that around midnight, you came out of the house in order to check what was happening in the neighbourhood, to check over the wall. So could you please tell me what is true; were you keeping watch or did you go out in order to look over the wall to see what was happening in the neighbourhood? What is the true version?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: It's the same truth. I -- from the yard, in fact, I heard a rifle, the sound made by an automatic rifle. So whether on guard in the yard or on guard in the house, it's really the same. It's all the same incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 1, in passage two of your first statement, you said that you heard a noise as if somebody was trying to break through the gate with a car. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes. That happened after I heard the automatic rifle being filled. And then I was in a room -- went to a room to inform Hani and Lulezim that something was happening, and then they broke the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your first statement, you said that you heard the noise of somebody trying to break through the gates with the cars. In your second statement, you say that you heard the sound of a weapon being loaded, and then, once you came into the house, you heard somebody say in Serbian, "Open the door." What was it you actually heard? Could you describe to me, please, what you heard.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: As I said, as soon as I heard the weapon being loaded, I went to the room and then the gate was broken in. In fact, the car only tried to break down the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which house were you in at that time?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: We were in the house of Lulezim Vejsa. It's a yard in which there are two houses. One is -- one has a basement, and the other one is an ordinary house where we sat during the day. And we've lived there all our lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there with you in the house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Besides the 21 members of our family in the basement, myself, Hani Hoxha, and Lulezim Vejsa were in the ordinary house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the women and children, at the time when you were fleeing the house, they were in another house, in the other house, in the basement, when you were escaping from the first house where you were. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the women and children at the time when you were escaping from the house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: They were in the basement of the other house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, in your first statement you say that you escaped from the house together with Lulezim and Hani Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You escaped through holes in the wall which had been prepared in advance. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your second statement, however, on page 3, in paragraph 5, you say something else. You claim that you escaped through the window of Lulezim's bedroom and then you jumped over the wall and went to another house. What is true?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: It's the same truth. It's the same version. I went in and then we jumped over the wall -- through the bedroom and over the wall, and went on. And the wall was -- had -- was partially destroyed, which we had prepared to make our escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your first statement, you say that Hani was walking behind you and Lulezim, but in your second statement you say that you didn't see Hani again until the morning. Was he with you or was he not with you?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: It's not true. After we fled, Hani remained somewhere behind us, whereas Lulezim and I were always together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You say that you hid in a nearby house. How far is that house from the house that you escaped from?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: About 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was half a kilometre away that you went. Something is not clear to me here. You say in your statement that you passed through several courtyards and hid in a house that wasn't inhabited, but a little while ago, you said, "In a nearby house," and now you're saying it was a house that was half a kilometre away from the house you escaped from. What is actually correct?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: This is a consistent truth. There's nothing to be disputed here. To go through 500 metres, you have to cross several yards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were in a nearby house, as you say, did you hear anything in the course of that night before you returned to your own house? Because you say in the first statement that in the morning, you came back to your house and you found that it was burnt. What did you hear during the night about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything. But we noticed that -- because the night was very dark, we noticed that some houses were burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your second statement something a little different. Awhile ago you said what I just quoted to you, that in the morning you came back to your house and found it was burnt. In the second statement: "While I was approaching, I saw that Vejsa's house was burning or that smoke was coming from it." Could you please answer: In which house were your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: They were sleeping in the basement. From the basement, according to the witness statement, the statement of the witness who experienced the incident, they say they took them from the basement and took them to the house, to the house where Lulezim and I had been staying, that is, to the ordinary house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You are referring to the statement given by this (redacted); right? Tell me, since you did not answer me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it will be redacted. No need to refer to that statement. You know that. Yes. Just deal with the witness -- what the witness found. Where did you find your wife and children, or where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't interrupt for a moment, please. Let the witness give his account.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to the statement of the person who survived, I found them at the very place where he told me they were, just as he described. They had been killed on the doorstep. My mother-in-law, my wife, my son. Whereas the other persons were executed in the other room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand your statement correctly, they were -- I asked you in which house were your -- were the women in children, in your house or in Vejsa's house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: In the Vejsas' house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your first statement, when you were describing your return, you say, "It wasn't the house that mattered. I was concerned about my family members." Are you talking about your house or Vejsa's house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I am talking about the Vejsas' house, because at that moment, it wasn't important whose house it was. The important thing was to -- for people to survive, the people who were left there to survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to have some things clarified here, because in the second statement you say: "I entered Vejsa's house that was full of rubble, that was still on fire." So what is correct? Whose house was on fire? Whose house did you enter? On the basis of what you've just said, it's Vejsa's house; right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: But these houses are within the same yard. Everything we are discussing about the event in question happened in the same yard. In fact, the basement where the family was in, the place -- the basement where they slept was only three metres away from the house where they used to live during the day, the ordinary house. I am speaking about the house of Lulezim Vejsa, which is a property -- unified property, so to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your second statement, you say that on that occasion, you talked to (redacted), who said to you that the Serb policemen entered the cellar, killed your nearest and dearest, and then set the place on fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I say that in your second statement, on page 4, paragraph 1, you say that when you talked to (redacted), who said to you that the Serb policemen came into the cellar, killed your nearest and dearest, and then torched the house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Milosevic chooses to use as his line of cross-examination this testing of the minute details of the witness's statements, that is Mr. Milosevic's prerogative. However, the Prosecution would only ask that it be done accurately. The last question of the accused was this: "You said that, according to a particular person, that the Serb police came to the basement, killed your nearest and dearest, and then burned the house." That is not what that paragraph, which is the first paragraph on page 4 of Mr. Haxhiavdija's second statement, reflects. What that paragraph says was: "He told me Serb police had come to the basement, taken them to the house and killed them." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You must take care, Mr. Milosevic, to put what the statement says. Mr. Haxhiavdija, you've heard what counsel has read out; that you talked to somebody, he told you he'd been in that basement with all the others, "He told me Serb police had come to the basement, taken them to the house and killed them." Is that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And when he referred to coming to the basement, so we can follow it, which basement was he referring to as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the family was sleeping in the basement there. According to the witness, they came, woke my family up, took all of them and sent them to the house, the ordinary house where they lived during the day, and that's where they executed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the house is the house that's referred to as Vejsa's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's the property of the Vejsa family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in relation to this objection, I am quoting what I mentioned a minute ago only to show to you that the quotation was quite precise. It says here: "Then I talked to --" and then this person whose name is redacted. "He had been in that basement with all the others. He told me Serb policemen had come to the basement, taken them to the house, and killed them. He told me that the policemen had killed another woman," et cetera. But the passage I quoted was an exact quotation. So we've established that. Now I'm moving on to your first statement. This had been the second statement. In the first statement, you do not mention this person at all, the person that we do not refer to in public session by name. You say that your former neighbour, whose name is redacted, two days upon your arrival in Tirana -- that is to say, two days upon your arrival in Tirana, told you who killed your family and how. Now, which version is correct, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Both are true. Both of them have to do with the same event. But first of all, because I was so angry and sad about what had happened, I went there in order to confirm the events. But some days later, we met in Tirana and there details were given about who committed all these crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your first statement, on page 3, in paragraph 6, "According to what he said to me --" you're referring to the neighbour you met in Tirana -- "I think that the following had happened." So according to what this neighbour had told you in Tirana, you think that the following had happened. And then you explain: "The Serb police and civilians took the members of my family out of the basement of Lulezim Vejsa, my wife's brother. They shot them and then they torched the house. Some used revolvers, others used automatic weapons. One of the children, Sihana Vejsa, six years old, was taken all the way to the cupboard where he was burned and killed." Then there's something that's redacted that is omitted, and then this person said, "One of the policemen had said, 'You've killed enough. Let's go on.'" And then again you say: "I think they were all in uniform. Almost a year before that, when it all started, all the men, all Serb men wore uniforms or were given uniforms," et cetera. So the conclusion as to what had happened and how is something that you draw on the basis of what your former neighbour said to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: The truth is what I described very well. I do not know what kind of interpretation you're having, but as far as I see, you're having -- you're getting a different interpretation of things. I told you, on the 2nd of April I met Dreni -- I met the person who survived and was wounded. He told me how the events had happened, how it came about when my kids were killed and then when they killed a young woman and an old woman and everybody else. However, the statement was as you said; he recognised the people, he saw them wearing uniforms. However, when he came to bigger details, also considering that he was unable to speak because he was bleeding and he needed help, he needed medical assistance, I ran to see whether I could do something for him. Correction: I ran for look for medical help. Some days later, we met in Tirana and he gave more details. He also identified the persons who had committed this criminal act.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Please tell me, is what you say in your first statement correct, namely that that person whose name we do not mention now, together with all the others who had been killed, was allegedly in the basement and that is how he told you about all of this? Was he in the basement?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: He was with all the other members of the family who slept in the basement. From there, they were sent to that house and were executed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did he tell you how come he survived?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he then manage to survive if they took people out of the basement or shot them there, killed them there? How did he manage to survive?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: He was wounded in his left hand. Apparently he was lucky and survived. You can ask that to him whenever you come face-to-face to him, if you will get a chance to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your first statement, on page 3 you mention the names of several persons as persons who were standing, drunk, that night by the house where your nearest and dearest were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: This is true, based on the statement that was given to me by another person, a person who actually lives in front of the Vejsas' house and could observe from his house whatever was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If I understood this correctly, you are inferring this on the basis of the fact that there was a cafe across the street and that there were beer bottles on the window sill or something like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: But there are plenty of coffee bars. However, none of them was open because of the curfew. In fact, the whole town was paralysed. No one could open any shops or anything. So they only took things or just had things with them, things they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you think that it is sufficient, on the basis of the fact that somebody is, for example, nearby drinking beer and the fact that this person left a beer bottle on a window sill, is that enough to infer that it was the same people who walked into your house, killed your family, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes, it's true, because they saw the people, and whoever was out there was identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who identified them? Was it the same person that you keep referring to all the time or was it somebody else who identified them? He told you that in Tirana; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: The person who told that to me in Tirana told me who had been there that night, referring to the persons who had committed the crime on my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of that is one and the same person that you keep quoting, right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. It's not the same person. The other person, I told you, used to live in the front of the Vejsas' house, and he identified the persons who were there who were in front of the shop that night and who entered the house and committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that that person had seen those other persons in front of the coffee bar. But that doesn't mean that those persons had killed someone. As far as I understand things, these persons were drinking beer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is going to be -- just a moment, Mr. Haxhiavdija. Mr. Milosevic, this is something we're going to have to decide. What we have is the witness's evidence on the point. He's given us -- he's told us what he has been told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But in your second statement, on page 4, paragraph 9, you blame the mayor of Djakovica, Stojanovic, directly for the death of your wife and children. Why are you accusing him now? Was he perhaps seen by some of your witnesses too? Was he also seen going there to kill your family?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No, he was not seen killing them, but he is - how do I put this? - the mastermind of these things or, rather, the person who allowed these things to happen in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the basis of the fact that a murder occurred in town, it is your assessment that the mayor, the president of the municipality, is responsible; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you came to the Vejsa house, did you see the killed persons?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I could not observe dead people -- correction, killed people, because nothing was left. When I went there, I could only see some parts and bits the flesh, what was left of the burned bodies and killed bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see Hysen Gashi's body, for example, that morning when you returned to the house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I also saw Hysen Gashi, observed Hysen Gashi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Hysen Gashi's body look like?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Only the body of Hysen Gashi was slightly more preserved than the others, but the other ones were unable to be identified. In Hysen Gashi's body, only the left part of the body was identifiable as a dead body. But otherwise, the feet, legs, and the arms were completely burned, even the bones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Haxhiavdija. What you describe - namely the rubble, then the body of Hysen Gashi was a charred body; right? - could that have been done by a bomb, all of that?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Not in any way, because the Vejsas' is -- in fact, the roof is almost adjacent to a Serbian house and not even the smallest window of this other house was broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not proof. I'm asking you about the house that you saw where your family had lost their lives. Could that house have been hit by a bomb?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. Because as I said, this Serbian house is only half a metre away from the Vejsas' house, and this house suffered no damage at all. And the walls of the houses -- the walls of the house were damaged by flame too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered the house, did the house have a roof?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that lead you to the assumption that perhaps it had been hit by a bomb?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. No way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is exclusively on the basis of the fact that the adjacent house had not been damaged?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's one way of showing this. But as I said, the walls of the house were still untouched, apart from one that fell in and the things that were burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Djakovica was bombed incessantly as of the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No, not at all. I experienced this time, and the first NATO bomb was dropped on the barracks, and after that there was no other bombing. On the 2nd of April, I then went to Albanian territory, to the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you claim that there was no bombing except for once, only one time when the barracks were targeted? Is it your claim that Djakovica was not bombed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: As long as I was there, according to what I experienced, I only saw this one bombing, and I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Djakovica? The 3rd of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us just be very precise. You claim that there was no bombing between the 24th of March until the 2nd of April. No bombing whatsoever except that one bomb that fell on the barracks.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, and as I said, we only saw the bomb on the barracks and I noticed no other explosions, large explosions, of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The way in which your family was killed or the fact that you say that this was committed by Serbs, police officers and civilians, do you base your conclusion exclusively on this witness whose name is not mentioned, and you have no other elements in order to base your claim on how your family was killed?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. The witness identified who was there, who was in the house and when they got them out of the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's this one witness on whose evidence you rely on and whose name was redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is all a matter of argument. Now, you have one minute left, so time for one last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, there is no need to repeat this argument. We've heard your evidence. The accused has one more question to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell me the following: You worked as a director of a company in Djakovica, and you were treated as a prominent citizen throughout the time until the war. What could have been the motive for anybody to break into your house and to come and murder your family? Did you ever think about that in order to determine who was it who committed that?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: You have the criminals in Serbia. You can find out yourself very easily. I have no reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have the amicus any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Behar, a little while ago you heard Prosecutor Saxon, in reading the brief resume of what you stated, said that you told them that that night you heard explosions. Is this true?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any explosions that night, the way that Mr. Saxon said awhile ago, how you stated that? Perhaps you said that to them. There is no mention of this in your statement, but Mr. Saxon read out awhile ago something relating to this, that perhaps in conversations with them you told them that you heard explosions in the course of that night. Did you hear explosions or did you not?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, Mr. Saxon didn't say that there had been any explosion, and I said that there were no explosions at all that night except that I saw flames rising from the house where I had been staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to repeat that I did hear Mr. Saxon say that. However, I don't insist on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It merely confuses the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge May, I have no intention of confusing the witness. In his statement, in his first statement, dated the 15th of April, 1999, the witness said that NATO began their air attacks and that this went on for five or six nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for five or six nights in a row, as you said, NATO bombed Djakovica. This is in paragraph 2 of your first statement.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, the bombing started on the 24th, not on the 15th of April, as you said. But as I said, I only heard --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say the 15th of April. You gave your statement on the 15th of April, 1999, and you said that NATO started the bombing, and when the bombing started, they bombed for five or six nights in a row. It's in paragraph 2 of your first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what are you trying to achieve by the cross-examination, please? Could you just explain to us what it is you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, awhile ago, in response to Mr. Milosevic's questions, he said there was only one bomb that was dropped, and his father also said that bombs were dropped five or six nights in a row, and in his statement he said that not only one bomb was dropped but the bombing went on for five or six nights in a row.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Can you help us, Mr. Haxhiavdija, about that? Which of those accounts is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The bombing started in general, but after the bombing started, the terror intensified every night. And I don't know what my father said because I wasn't close to my father there. But on the 24th I only heard that one bomb. There may be other bombs that fell outside the city which we didn't hear at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I can conclude, then, that you only heard one bomb and nothing more?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in your second statement, of May 7th 2001 - in the English version this is on page 2, the last paragraph - you also said that the bombing started a week before April 1st. And in the last sentence, you said that during the day, nobody went down to the basement during the day. You were in your family houses, and at night you went down to the basement in Vejsa's house to sleep. Was this done because NATO bombing was conducted generally at night? It was a well-known fact that NATO bombs were dropped only at night, and that this is why you went down to the basement.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. No, that was not the reason. But all the beds were down there to sleep at night, whereas during the day, we spent the time in the ordinary house, living reasonably normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is the Vejsa house from your house, and was the basement in your house suitable for you to be able to spend the night there?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: My house didn't have a cellar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can answer just this one more question: Were you able to look into the basement of Vejsa's house after everything that had happened to the house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't there at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The house was knocked down?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: The house was demolished totally, including the roof and all the contents. They were all burned entirely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more thing: Awhile ago you said that you went inside the house. No?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I went into the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, why did you originally decide to bring your family to your brother-in-law's house, Mr. Vejsa's house, on Milos Gilic Street?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Because my house is an old one, built about 50 or 60 years ago, and it wasn't really safe because it didn't have a cellar. And we thought that people from Cabrat might come and attack our house, and we didn't feel safe so we decided to go to the Vejsas'.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "people from Cabrat," could you be more specific, please? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: I'm talking about the police and the army who had positioned their heavy artillery on the Cabrat Hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the army," you're referring to the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is your house located close to Cabrat Hill?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Milosevic suggested that your brother-in-law's house was struck by bombs, that NATO bombs had struck the area on the 2nd of April. I'd like to show you a photograph, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask the usher's assistance to distribute the photograph, please. There should be enough copies. And a copy could please be placed on the ELMO so that everyone can look on. Place it on the ELMO. That's good. Thank you. Mr. Haxhiavdija -- can we raise up the projector just a bit so we get a slightly higher view? Just a bit, please. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes. It's Milos Gilic Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pick up a pen or a pointer, please, and point to the compound of your brother-in-law, Mr. Vejsa, where your family and others had taken shelter on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: The family were sheltering in this building, which was strong and built of strong materials. Here was the cellar. It was from here that the people were taken and brought to this house here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your brother-in-law's house, Mr. Vejsa's house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this is the entire property of the Vejsa family, from these four corners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please pick up a pen, or if there is no pen there you can take my pen, and write the letter -- write an arrow and the letter "B," pointing to the basement where the women and children had taken shelter.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: This was the basement. And this was the house where people lived normally during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put the letter "H," which would stand for "house" in English, by that spot, please.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haxhiavdija, would this photo depict the Milos Gilic Street neighbourhood before the war in 1999 or after?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: This shows the street after the war, or after the events that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Haxhiavdija, I know that a number of your relatives lived in that house on Milos Gilic Street. Did you have occasion to visit that house from time to time before the war?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the -- did you get to know, at least by sight, the neighbours who lived on that street besides your brother-in-law and his family?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I knew some of them. I recognised some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know the ethnicity of some of the neighbours who lived on that street?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes. There were Romanies, there were Serbs, and Montenegrins, and Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, could you place your pointer on your brother-in-law's compound, please.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a house that appears to be undamaged directly behind the compound of the Vejsa family. Do you see that house? It's directly behind the house where you were.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of the family who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: They were Albanians. In fact, two people from that house slept in our house, and one of them was killed in the massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Haxhiavdija, moving one house to the right of that compound, Mr. Vejsa's house, we see another house that apparently is undamaged. Could you place your pen on that house to the right, please.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of the family who lived in that house?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes, there were Serbs here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we go one house to the right, please. Who lived in that next house to the right? Was it a Serb family, an Albanian family, or other?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: They were Romanies here, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the house to the right of that, do you know whether that was a Serb family or an ethnic Albanian family or other?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: This here is the house of the person who survived the incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would be an Albanian family?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's an Albanian house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the house to the right of that?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: This one is a Serbian house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Haxhiavdija, can we go, please, to the homes that are across the street from Lulezim Vejsa's house. We see a lot of damage there. Do you see those homes?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The homes that are directly across the street from Mr. Vejsa's house. What was the ethnicity of those three homes where we see a lot of damage, the ethnicity of the families who lived there?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: They were Albanian houses here and here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were any of the houses that were damaged on that street, did any of them belong to Serb families?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: No. Those houses have remained undamaged down to the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if Mr. Milosevic is correct that this damage was caused by NATO bombing, somehow the NATO bombing only damaged homes inhabited by Albanians; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: That's what he seems to think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Just for the record, Your Honour, this photo is also in evidence in the Milos Gilic Street binder, which is Exhibit 160, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be -- just a moment. It may be convenient to give it another number so it can be attached to this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 304.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding these new facts, I would say these new facts which Mr. Saxon is trying to interpret in the wrong way here, Mr. Haxhiavdija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to ask some further questions, you better ask permission first. You can't just launched into a further examination. You can ask, since this photograph wasn't produced, you can ask questions for two minutes about it, but no more. Further cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You indicated the house where the basement was where the members of your family were hiding. As we can see, that house is untouched. It wasn't burned. It wasn't demolished. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: It shows that there was no bombing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was bombing there.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: There was no bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. I am just saying that the house where the basement was was not burned. You said that the house with the basement and where your relatives were killed was all under -- in rubble and that it was burned. Here we see that the house is standing and that it wasn't set on fire.

utterances.speaker: BEHAR HAXHIAVDIJA
utterances.text: This house was built of very strong materials, and there was not a thing to burn in it except the basement where the beds and other things for the night were put. That was burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I am not disputing the possibility that the house was burned. I am doubting your claim that you came and found charred bodies in the house. Now in the photograph we see that the house was not burnt. It hasn't been damaged at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are misrepresenting the evidence, Mr. Milosevic. The evidence which the witness gave was that the bodies were not in the house with the basement. They had been taken from there and taken to the house which he's identified, which we can see destroyed, to the right in the same compound. Now, that is the damaged building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. We'll check the transcript, but this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it evident in the houses that have been demolished that all the walls are white, there are no traces of a fire except for this one up here on the corner, so it's probably then the effect of bombardment and not of any burning. Had they been set on fire, the walls would be black or at least there would be traces of fire on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the witness deal with that. What is suggested is that you can't see the trace of fire, so this damage which we can see in the photograph, 304, must be the result of bombing. Now, this will be the last question. Mr. Haxhiavdija, can you deal with that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you can see the traces. Of course you can. You can see the burning. If you come closer, you will see that all the walls are burned and damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He may have been referring -- the accused may have been referring to the houses which are lower down in the photograph. If you look to the house to the right there, it looks as though there's burning there. But I'm not -- no, I'm not going to go on because it will be a matter for us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Just because Mr. Saxon tried to manipulate with the fact and to come out with an assumption of how the Albanian houses and not Serbian houses were burned and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you mark on this photograph all the houses that are Serb houses. I would like to keep this in order to check this. Regardless of the fact if they were destroyed or not. Could you please indicate all the Serb houses. How many of them did you mark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's marked them on the overhead. And while you're at it, perhaps, Mr. Haxhiavdija, you would mark the Albanian houses with an "A", please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many Serb houses did you mark, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about these houses here that are left untouched? Are they all Serbian or Albanian? And what was the percentage of the Serb population in Djakovica, Mr. Haxhiavdija?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we are going to bring this to an end, otherwise we shall never finish. Could you just mark the Albanian houses, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And these with "A" are Albanians, and with "S" are Serbian houses, and "R" means a Romany house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as we can see, more Albanian houses are left standing than Serbian houses, even in this part that was destroyed. And these destroyed houses that you can see, which ones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, eventually your examination must to come to an end. It cannot go on forever. You've been given more time. The witness has marked on the map the various things, and there's no point continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I wonder if you can help us with when and by whom this picture was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This picture was taken, Your Honour, I believe by one of the investigators working for the OTP. I do not have the exact date. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was taken by representatives of the FBI, the Federal Bureau of Investigation from the United States. We don't have the date handy at this time, but we can get it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would appreciate that. Please get the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Haxhiavdija, at the end of it all there's a simple matter of fact. During the night on your family were killed, did a bomb fall on Milos Gilic Street, on any of the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no bomb fell, but there was burning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we have been reflecting on the last witness, and we're concerned about the photograph production at the last minute. And thinking about it, of course acknowledging that it is easier to deal with these things with hindsight than beforehand, it really would have been better, we think, if the photograph had been produced early on. Now, we know it's part of the material which was part of the binder, and therefore it was disclosed and anybody could have had it, but given the amount of material in this case, anyone can be forgiven for not immediately connecting everything up. So acknowledging too the limitations of time which you're under, if there is a case in which there may be an issue of that sort, it would be helpful to have the exhibit at the beginning rather than the end. And that's not only in the interests of fairness, so that the accused can have it, decide to take instructions on it, it's also in the interests of our following the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. And with regard to that same exhibit, 304, Judge Kwon asked me to provide the date and source of the photograph. This photograph was taken by the FBI War Crimes Task Force when this body was conducting investigations in Kosova, between the 24th of June, 1999 and the 29th of June, 1999. So the photo was taken during that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the marked copy of the photograph will be given Prosecutor's Exhibit 304A. And a clarification for witness Haxhiavdija's statement; 303A will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will now call Mr. Izet Krasniqi. While we're waiting, Your Honours, Mr. Krasniqi's evidence will be relevant to page 06 of the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Trial Chamber's permission, I have Mr. Krasniqi's name spelled correctly. If that could be exhibited or, excuse me, displayed on the ELMO, please. Examined by Mr. Saxon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Izet Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, were you born on the 1st of March, 1942, in the village of Studime e Poshtme in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that village located in the municipality of Vushtrri, to the east of the town of Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, on the 30th of March, 2000, did you provide a statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosova in 1999?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 11th of October, 2001, did you provide an additional statement to a member of the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you witnessed and experienced in Kosova in 1999?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 2nd of February of this year, 2002, in Kosova, were you provided with copies of the statements that you previously gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in a language that you understand in the presence of a member of the Office of the Prosecutor and a presiding officer appointed by the Registry?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, true. The statement was read to me by the investigators of the Tribunal, but copies were not given to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But did you confirm that the copies that were read to you were true and correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would ask that the statements of Mr. Krasniqi be distributed but that they not be marked for admission yet because I have a question or two that I have to discuss with this witness regarding one of his statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, recently in conversations with me here in The Hague, did you observe some mistakes in the statement that you provided on the 30th of March, 2000?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first full paragraph on page 5 of the English version of your statement of 30 March 2000, and also on page 5 of the Serbian version, you describe how thousands of displaced people had gathered in the village of Studime e Eperme on the 2nd of May, 1999, when Serb forces broke through KLA resistance. In the last sentence of that paragraph, you say that: "We decided to stay even though we had no reliable information from the KLA." Is that last sentence correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. We had no sure information, and we couldn't even believe what was happening to us. As far as the Serb forces were concerned, we didn't know whether they were going to fight with the KLA or whether there was something worse that could happen to the population, the innocent population, unarmed population which was being misplaced from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, what if anything did members of the KLA say to the people that were gathered in Studime e Eperme at that time?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The KLA advised us that since we were unarmed people, we should just stick to the convoy we were in because if the Serb forces would come along, it was expected that they might attack us. But we were the innocent people, and if they were a fair, normal army, then they wouldn't attack us. So we had to stay in the convoy so as to prevent what happened to us from happening. But before the Serb forces came, we gathered, a group of people gathered. We discussed amongst ourselves, and we decided that on the 2nd of May, around 3.00 -- the following persons were present in that gathering: Bajram Mulaku --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, did the KLA say anything else to you and the group you were with before you joined the convoy on the 2nd of May? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The army advised us, since we were not armed and we were innocent, they said if they want to attack someone, they will come and look for the KLA. They told us, "You are the innocent, unarmed population. We will just create a corridor for you through which you will pass," as opposed to the difficulties we went through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krasniqi, on page 8 of the English version of the same statement, it's also page 8 of the Serbian version, in the middle of the page, you say that you remained in Albania until the 1st of September, when you were able to return to Kosova. Is that sentence correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I corrected it. Not 1st of September, but it was on 1st of August that I returned from Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with those corrections, I would offer the statement of Mr. Krasniqi into evidence under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the original will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 305, under seal, and the public redacted version will be 305A.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Izet Krasniqi, a Kosovo Albanian Muslim, was born and previously resided in the village of Studime e Poshtme in the Vushtrri municipality. His house in the village was burned down in 1999. By the 26th of March, 1999, it became too dangerous in the village, so the witness went with his wife and son to stay with relatives in the town of Vushtrri. Whilst Mr. Krasniqi stayed in Vushtrri, Serb paramilitary burned houses and the main mosque in the centre of the town. On or about the 5th or 6th of April, 1999, Serbian paramilitary evicted Mr. Krasniqi and his relatives from Vushtrri, giving them five minutes to leave. His relatives left for Macedonia, but the witness returned with his family to his village of Studime e Poshtme. Mr. Krasniqi describes Serb paramilitaries setting up a base around the 15th of April, 1999, on a hill close to and overlooking his village. These forces had tanks, mortars, and automatic weapons. Mortar and sniper fire was directed at Mr. Krasniqi's village and homes were damaged. On the 20th of April, 1999, a woman and her daughter were shot by snipers. Mr. Krasniqi describes daily shelling of Studime e Poshtme and alleges that people were killed by snipers, including a woman and daughter. One day, Mr. Krasniqi and his family fled their home due to heavy shelling. That day, Mr. Krasniqi's home was completely destroyed. Eventually, about 10.000 displaced persons were gathered in and around Studime e Poshtme. After paramilitaries shot several persons, the refugees decided to go higher in the mountains, to the village of Studime e Eperme, for safety. Mr. Krasniqi and his family arrived there on his tractor early in the morning of 20 April. There was a KLA presence in Studime e Eperme, but on 1 May 1999, word arrived that Serb forces had broken through the KLA resistance. Eventually, about 25.000 displaced persons gathered in Studime e Eperme. As the Serb forces advanced, the KLA soldiers left the area. Around 7.00 p.m. on the 2nd of May, as Serb forces approached from the north, west, and east, the refugees formed a convoy of tractors and trailers four to five kilometres long that began to move toward Studime e Poshtme to the south. Serb forces fired at the convoy, and Mr. Krasniqi's wife was wounded in the leg. While Mr. Krasniqi tried to help her, Serb forces on foot and in tanks and Pinzgauers caught up with his part of the convoy. Mr. Krasniqi was forced to turn over 300 Deutschmarks to one paramilitary and another paramilitary struck him on the head with the barrel of his gun. Mr. Krasniqi became separated from his wife and continued to drive his tractor in the convoy. At one moment, Mr. Krasniqi saw a Serb paramilitary in a Pinzgauer vehicle aiming a grenade launcher at him. The grenade hit Mr. Krasniqi's tractor and exploded. Mr. Krasniqi was thrown to the ground and suffered wounds to his forehead and left shoulder and his left arm was broken. Eventually, he crawled into a covered trailer being pulled by another tractor. At around 11.00 p.m., Mr. Krasniqi reached the agricultural cooperative outside of the town of Vushtrri. The next morning, Serb paramilitaries ordered all of the men between 18 and 60 to gather on one side of the compound. Mr. Krasniqi remained inside the trailer. The paramilitaries forced the Kosovo Albanian men to stand with their hands on their heads and shout "Slobo" and "Draskovic." Two large trucks arrived and the men were forced to climb into them and were taken away. The paramilitaries told the remaining Kosovo Albanians to get back onto their trailers and drive onto the main road. Mr. Krasniqi rode in the trailer as it passed through Mitrovica and was stopped at roadblocks in Skenderaj, Istok, Klina, and Xerxe. At each roadblock, Serb paramilitaries forced the people on each tractor to turn over at least 100 Deutschmarks. The driver of Mr. Krasniqi's tractor was beaten at these roadblocks. At the Albanian border crossing at Morina in the Gjakove municipality, a Serb policeman and a Serb soldier questioned the occupants of Mr. Krasniqi's trailer. The Serb forces took all of the identity cards and passports from the Kosovo Albanians before allowing them to cross the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated in your first statement that you always worked in the administration and that from 1998, you worked in the accounting service of the Obilic thermoelectric power plant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Albanians were employed at the Obilic thermoelectric power plant?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The former electrical plant, since 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, what are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The events that we went through but also some database from our past which I have jotted down regarding workers and employees which the accused asked about. In 1990, there were 11.000 Albanian -- Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 9355 to 9368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You're giving evidence here, and the normal rule is that witnesses don't give evidence from notes but, of course, from their recollection. But you say you have a note, do you, as to those who were employed in the power plant? You've got a note about that, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have notes in general about the thermoelectric power plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can use those notes, but apart from that, would you not use them unless there's a specific point you want to refresh your memory on. Yes. Now, give us the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear. In the thermoelectric power plant, 70 per cent of the employees were Albanian, which, generally speaking, in Kosova at the time, 90 per cent of the population was Albanian, and we deserved to have 70 per cent of Albanian employees in the plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's another point. If you would just concentrate on the questions and just give the answers, we'll get on more quickly. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the total number of employees at the thermoelectric power plants at Obilic?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: In total, up until violence started, their number was around 12.000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So thousands and thousands of Albanians worked at the thermoelectric power plants in Obilic all the way up to the war. Isn't that right, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember when the members of the KLA, during 1998, abducted a group of workers employed at the thermoelectric power plant, and they were going to work at the pit at Belacevac?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Of which nationality are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They abducted a group of Serbs, workers who were working in the pit, in the Belacevac pit. If you remember their names, they were Dragan Vukomirovic, Zoran Anicic, Petar Acancic, Dusan Acancic, Miroslav Trifunovic, Sebera Sabic [phoen], Bozidar Lencic, and Marijan Buha. Of course, in Belacevac, for the most part it was Albanians who were employed there, but the persons abducted were Serbs. They were workers who were going to do their shift in the pits. That was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I remember what you're talking about. I do not remember the names and surnames. I remember the kidnapping, but I do not know who they were kidnapped by, and I do not know why they were kidnapped. But Serb forces were conducting large operations, wide operations in Kosovo, and all the kidnappings and the killings and everything happened because of them and by them. The accused knows that very well as far as they are concerned, as far as everything is concerned in Kosovo. However, the bottom line is I do not know who kidnapped them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember, perhaps, that the kidnapping of these workers was the first incident in the area and that this could not have been caused by any operations of the Serb forces, as you had put it? Do you remember that, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Since 1990, when violent measures also included the thermoelectrical plant, discrimination within the administration reached high levels, and Lazar Ecevic, Milan Vujakovic, and a person by the name of Sokrat, who was Roman, were also conducting discrimination, so to say. He also worked in the Serb administration, who kept discriminating Albanians, kicking them out of their jobs and violating their employment rights and their rights to -- their right to exist, merely because they had the power and the administration in their hands. While we Albanians, we loved working. Even though economically speaking we were not very well off, however, the desire to survive and to work honestly. Regardless of all these, we underwent killing and execution and discrimination. 137 employees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, we must keep these within bounds. Can you answer the questions as shortly as possible. Mr. Milosevic, we will not be assisted by political argument, which these sort of questions lead to. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of discrimination are you speaking about, Mr. Krasniqi? When we stated a few minutes ago that thousands and thousands of Albanians worked at the thermoelectric power plants in Obilic only. You're even talking about killings and I don't know what all. What kind of discrimination are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was discrimination. People were sacked. When the war started on a large scale, the Albanians suffered in comparison with the structure of the Serbian population. This was outright discrimination. It was disproportionate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Krasniqi. These are rather general statements that are refuted by facts. And do you know about the fate of these kidnapped workers who were also going to their work peacefully, going to work in the mine? And their fate remains unknown. Nothing is known about them up to the present day.

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear that, after the kidnapping, they were transferred to the KLA prison in Likovac in Drenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know about prisons because the KLA didn't have prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim that the KLA did not have any prisons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I don't know of the KLA having any prisons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you think? Through the efforts of the Verification Mission of the OSCE, where were soldiers who had been kidnapped released from, for example, or journalists who had been released? The negotiations on their release took days. Where were they released from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is no point arguing about this. He says he doesn't know. He says the KLA didn't have any prisons. Now, you can produce your evidence on the point in due course, but there's no point arguing with him about it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that in that period, during 1998 in particular, there were many breakdowns and many attacks at various stations in Obilic, then also transmission lines were broken, machinery was stopped, bombs were planted. There were sabotages, et cetera. Do you know about that? Because you were employed there all the time.

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At that time, I don't know of there being breakdowns, as you claim. And even if there were, it was all in the hands of the Serbian administration. We were not able to conduct any sabotage or cause any breakdowns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was well known in the public. Even the newspapers wrote about this, carried pictures. This was on television. So you don't remember any of this; right?

utterances.speaker: IZET KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I said, as I said before, Your Honours, that we had no authority to cause -- or we didn't have powers to cause sabotage or breakdowns in the Kosovar power network. And after the Serbian authorities took management into their hands, we were mainly -- we were merely manual workers, and we only had jobs that Serbs didn't like doing. So we were not in any position to cause any breakdowns because of this discrimination.
